situations.name: Typed error taxonomy
situations.definition: A developer needs to add or classify a fallible outcome so it crosses the IPC boundary as a structured, categorized, machine-branchable error rather than a string.
situations.note: Rust AppError kind/category and the TS mirror src/lib/errorTaxonomy.ts must stay in lockstep; nothing checks that today (grep of scripts/.github/lefthook finds no parity gate), so a new variant can silently classify as Unknown on the frontend.

situations.name: Secret and PII redaction
situations.definition: A developer is about to persist, log, or ship somewhere a string that may contain a credential or personal data, and needs the canonical scrubber for that egress point.
situations.note: FOUR independent implementations with four different pattern sets and thresholds: trace-persistence redaction (entropy sweep, kill-switchable), audit-log sanitize_secrets, Sentry pii::scrub, and IPC error-path stripping. A pattern added to one does not reach the others; a secret leaking through the weakest one is unrecoverable.

situations.name: Encrypting a secret at rest
situations.definition: A developer needs to store a credential, token, or trigger config in SQLite such that the row is useless without the machine's master key.
situations.note: Three near-identical entry points (encrypt_for_db / encrypt_field / encrypt_trigger_config) with different nonce-return shapes; nothing prevents a new sensitive column from being written in plaintext.

situations.name: Master key sourcing policy
situations.definition: A developer is deciding where the 32-byte encryption key comes from on a given platform and what happens when the OS keychain is unavailable.
situations.note: Fail-closed with three env escape hatches (PERSONAS_ALLOW_FALLBACK_KEY, PERSONAS_MIGRATE_LEGACY_KEY, DPAPI wrapping). Two documented bug-hunt findings came from the doc comment and the runtime branch having diverged; only Rust unit tests defend it, and they need --features desktop or the mobile stub compiles instead.

situations.name: In-memory secret lifetime
situations.definition: A developer holds a plaintext secret in process memory and needs it zeroized, un-swappable, and non-printable in Debug output.
situations.note: SecureString / EncryptedToken / ProtectedKey are the three primitives; nothing stops a new code path from binding a raw String. Memory-locking has three platform variants plus a no-op stub.

situations.name: IPC command authorization
situations.definition: A developer adds a Tauri command and must decide its auth tier and wire the guard so the frontend cannot invoke privileged work without the session token.
situations.note: Two mechanisms coexist — the wrap_invoke_handler privileged-command HashSet and the #[requires(level)] proc-macro. Nothing asserts a new sensitive command was added to the set; check-literal-parity.mjs was a one-off audit and is wired to no npm script, hook, or workflow.

situations.name: SSRF-safe outbound HTTP
situations.definition: A developer makes an HTTP request to a host influenced by user or credential data and needs the client that cannot reach loopback, RFC1918, CGNAT, or cloud-metadata.
situations.note: Three shared LazyLock clients where picking the wrong one is a silent SSRF hole; HTTP_ALLOW_PRIVATE is legal at exactly one call site by comment only. A previously divergent private-IP predicate in engine::ssrf_safe_dns was folded in after it drifted.

situations.name: Command input validation
situations.definition: A developer accepts a user-supplied id, name, or free-text field at the IPC boundary and needs the canonical whitelist/strip before it reaches SQL, a path, or storage.
situations.note: The module is `#![allow(dead_code)] // Used by commands as needed` — validation is opt-in per command with no mechanism telling a new command author which helper applies.

situations.name: Feature-flagged compilation
situations.definition: A developer adds code that must only compile in some build profiles (desktop / ML / P2P / test-automation / scraper) and has to declare and forward the Cargo feature correctly.
situations.note: 569 cfg sites across 95 files, and each feature must be re-declared and forwarded into personas-core/-db/-engine. Missing the forward silently compiles a stub (crypto's mobile keychain path). check-tauri-configs only validates that a config's feature NAME exists; CI compiles only `desktop`, so `ml`/`p2p`/`scraper`/`daemon`/`ollama` paths are never built by any gate.

situations.name: Crate layering discipline
situations.definition: A developer decides which workspace crate a new module belongs in so the dependency graph stays acyclic and rustc can parallelize.
situations.note: "personas-core may not depend on any other Personas crate" is prose in a doc comment. Enforced only by whether cargo happens to fail; several modules (limits, drive_root, ipc_gauge) exist purely to break a back-edge and would silently re-form it if someone re-imported.

situations.name: Compile-time env embedding
situations.definition: A developer needs a build-time constant (OAuth client id, Sentry DSN, Supabase key) baked into the shipped binary from .env.
situations.note: Explicit forward-list; adding an option_env! read without adding the key here silently ships an empty value. rerun-if-env-changed was added only after swatinem/rust-cache made a stale cached build script ship a rotated secret's old value.

situations.name: ts-rs binding export
situations.definition: A developer adds #[derive(TS)] to a Rust struct and needs the generated TypeScript to land in exactly one committed location.
situations.note: The export dir has been silently wrong three separate ways (.cargo/config.toml [env] not reaching proc-macro expansion; CI missing --workspace so ~200 core types went unchecked; run-rust-tests spawning exes from repo root so ts-rs dumped 419 files into a gitignored dir). The gate is real but has repeatedly checked nothing.

situations.name: Codegen task registration
situations.definition: A developer adds a generated artifact and needs it to run on every dev/build without serializing the startup path or hanging it.
situations.note: One flat explicit registry, per-task 60s timeout, Promise.allSettled. Trap: predev and prebuild have DIFFERENT task lists (checksums vs host-check) and any path bypassing npm (check-tiers spawning vite directly) must re-run codegen itself.

situations.name: Source-derived codegen
situations.definition: A developer needs one language's artifact generated from another language's source so the two can never drift by hand.
situations.note: Every generator hand-rolls a bespoke regex over source text — no shared parse layer. generate-command-names.mjs matches `invoke_handler\(tauri::generate_handler!\[` while lib.rs:1805 actually reads `wrap_invoke_handler(tauri::...` — it works only because one string is a substring of the other; check-command-contract.mjs matches the wrapped form. A wrapper rename breaks them differently.

situations.name: Cross-artifact drift gate
situations.definition: A developer has two artifacts that must agree (Rust handler vs TS union, Rust events vs TS registry, error keys vs locale keys) and needs a check that fails when they don't.
situations.note: Two shapes coexist: regenerate-and-git-diff (bindings, command names) vs independent re-derivation (contracts, event registry). The errorTaxonomy Rust↔TS mirror — arguably the most consequential pair — has NO gate of either shape.

situations.name: Adding a custom lint rule
situations.definition: A developer wants a repo convention machine-enforced in TS/TSX and needs to author, register, severity-tune, and test an ESLint rule.
situations.note: 21 rule files; customRules.test.ts covers only 12 (`ruleTester.run` count). Nine rules — including the newest ones — have zero regression coverage, so a regex edit can silently stop matching.

situations.name: Lint severity posture
situations.definition: A developer decides whether a new convention lands as error (blocking) or warn (advisory migration) and how the existing ~10k-warning baseline stays non-blocking.
situations.note: Only 3 of 21 custom rules are error-level. Pre-commit runs `--quiet --max-warnings 99999`, so warn-level rules gate nothing at all — 'ESLint enforces it' in CLAUDE.md is true for 3 rules and aspirational for 18.

situations.name: Git hook design
situations.definition: A developer wants a check to run automatically before commit or push without breaking the flow of concurrent CLI sessions sharing one tree.
situations.note: Hard constraints stated at the top: <5s pre-commit, never stash/mutate the tree. Glob-scoped jobs (i18n) only fire when locale files are staged, so the value-translation gate never runs on a commit that adds English-only JSX.

situations.name: Adding a CI gate
situations.definition: A developer wants a check enforced on the merge/push path and must place it in the right job, on the right runner, with the right feature flags.
situations.note: This file is a museum of gates that ran green while checking nothing: commit-lint died on `origin/..HEAD` on every push; `cargo test` aborted pre-compile without --features desktop; binding-drift skipped ~200 types without --workspace; an sccache outage took the whole Rust lane offline for weeks. The recurring failure mode is a gate that errors or no-ops instead of failing.

situations.name: Secret-leak scanning
situations.definition: A developer needs staged changes checked for credentials before they leave the machine, plus a way to triage historical hits.
situations.note: The gate exits 0 with a hint when gitleaks is not installed — a silently-passing control by design, and it is the ONLY secret scan in the repo (no CI leg). A fresh clone on a machine without gitleaks has zero leak protection.

situations.name: Supply-chain policy
situations.definition: A developer adds or bumps a dependency and needs the license, advisory, source-registry, and duplication policy applied.
situations.note: cargo-deny is a per-push gate for Rust; the npm side (security-audit.sh) runs only on a weekly cron, and CodeQL covers javascript-typescript only — Rust SAST is clippy plus deny by explicit decision.

situations.name: Windows loader and toolchain traps
situations.definition: A developer runs Rust tests or a build on Windows and hits a failure that is the loader or a mislabeled prebuilt artifact, not their code.
situations.note: Three distinct self-healing workarounds (comctl32 v6 post-link manifest, ORT aarch64 tarball swap, host-triple drift marker). CI runs Rust tests only via raw `cargo test` on Linux, so the Windows lane is untested by any gate — the trap it works around went undetected precisely because CI never sees it.

situations.name: Bundling native assets
situations.definition: A developer ships a non-Rust artifact (ONNX runtime, skill files, models, icons) with the installer and must guarantee the app can find it at runtime.
situations.note: The ONNX verifier had to become linking-aware (reads the PE import table) after hard-requiring a DLL false-failed every static build. Tauri validates bundle.resources paths in DEV too, so a resource dir that only prebuild creates breaks a fresh clone's `tauri dev` — solved by adding sync-system-skills to predev.

situations.name: Tier-gated build variants
situations.definition: A developer gates a feature behind a product tier and needs all three frontend bundles to still compile and tree-shake correctly.
situations.note: The gate proves each tier COMPILES, not that gating is correct — a feature leaking into starter passes. Ordering is load-bearing: check:tiers writes dist/ so it must run before the canonical build that later steps read.

situations.name: Tauri config overlays
situations.definition: A developer needs a build variant (lite/stable/android) that differs from the canonical Tauri config in a controlled, minimal way.
situations.note: Allowed overlay surface is exactly two keys (build.features, bundle.targets) with an explicit expand-intentionally comment. tauri.android.conf.json is NOT in the checked overlay list.

situations.name: Tauri capability permissions
situations.definition: A developer uses a Tauri plugin API and must declare its permission in the right capability file for the right platforms.
situations.note: Coupled to Cargo features in a non-obvious way: default.json names `updater:default`, whose plugin is an optional dep enabled only by `desktop`, so any cargo command without that feature aborts in tauri-build before compiling. That coupling silently disabled CI's entire Rust test job.

situations.name: Content Security Policy scope
situations.definition: A developer adds a remote origin (image CDN, media stream, embed, telemetry endpoint) and must widen the webview CSP and asset-protocol scope for it.
situations.note: Two hand-maintained ~1KB single-line CSP strings (prod + dev) that must be kept in sync by eye; no script validates them, no gate catches a prod/dev divergence, and a missing directive fails only at runtime in a packaged build.

situations.name: Release and version pipeline
situations.definition: A developer cuts a release and needs version files, tag, changelog, four platform builds, and updater artifacts to move together.
situations.note: Publishing is opt-in after auto-tagging left 5 tags with no releases behind them. Version lives in four files that must agree; the tag-collision guard exists because a rollback stranded every subsequent run 45 minutes into platform builds.

situations.name: Installer acceptance testing
situations.definition: A developer needs proof that the packaged installer actually installs, launches, and finds its runtime deps on a clean machine.
situations.note: Runs AFTER release, not before it — a broken installer is discovered post-publish. Promotion to a pre-release gate is a tracked step in the e2e-smoke ADR. macOS leg is smoke-only because the app is unsigned/un-notarized.

situations.name: Live UI test automation
situations.definition: A developer wants an external driver to click through the real running desktop app rather than a mocked DOM.
situations.note: Two activation paths (compile-time feature → :17320, env var → custom port) plus an MCP bridge. The only CI leg is `continue-on-error: true` with explicit promotion criteria never met, so this is enforcement-free today.

situations.name: Writing a Rust unit test
situations.definition: A developer adds a #[cfg(test)] module and needs it to actually build and run under the repo's feature flags and platform quirks.
situations.note: 514 test modules / ~14.6k #[test]. Local (npm run test:rust, --lib only, manifest fixup) and CI (raw cargo test, all targets) run DIFFERENT commands, so the two lanes can disagree about what passes. Feature-name qualification differs between the two lanes too.

situations.name: Rust test fixtures and DBs
situations.definition: A developer needs a database, temp directory, or process-global env var for a test without leaking state into the next test.
situations.note: Three coexisting strategies: init_test_db (unique temp FILE, because r2d2 breaks with :memory:), ad-hoc Connection::open_in_memory in 9 files, and a hand-rolled mutex around PERSONAS_HOME because env vars are process-global. No shared fixture crate; each area reinvents setup().

situations.name: Frontend test lane selection
situations.definition: A developer writes a test and must choose which of six runner configurations it belongs to, and whether any gate will run it.
situations.note: Six configs (unit/jsdom, cli, e2e, evals, integration, playwright). CI runs only `npm run test` (unit) — cli/integration/e2e configs have no gate at all; evals run on pre-push only. Placement decides whether a test is ever executed by anything.

situations.name: Persisted settings contract
situations.definition: A developer adds a user-configurable app setting and needs its key, default, unit, and validation to have one canonical home.
situations.note: The strongest convention in the slice: every key pairs with a <KEY>_DEFAULT, units live in the key name, and validate_key/validate_value are enforced inside the repo setter so internal callers can't bypass. Runtime-gated rather than CI-gated.

situations.name: Environment-variable configuration
situations.definition: A developer adds an env-var escape hatch (feature toggle, test port, override URL, migration opt-in) and needs it discoverable and consistently parsed.
situations.note: ~40 distinct PERSONAS_* / provider vars read via bare std::env::var at their point of use — no registry, no type parsing convention, no doc surface, no gate. Several change SECURITY behavior (PERSONAS_ALLOW_FALLBACK_KEY, PERSONAS_MIGRATE_LEGACY_KEY, PERSONAS_BROWSER_BRIDGE_TOKEN); a documented policy already drifted from its runtime branch once here.

situations.name: Structured logging and retention
situations.definition: A developer needs a runtime event recorded so it survives to a bug report, without unbounded disk growth or a boot-order dependency.
situations.note: Deferred file writer solves the real problem — the subscriber installs before the app-data dir is known, so early-boot lines would otherwise be lost or block. Retention enforced twice (on rotation and at startup) because the cap can shrink between runs.

situations.name: Telemetry scrubbing and opt-in
situations.definition: A developer needs a crash or error reported to Sentry without shipping PII, credentials, or debug-build noise.
situations.note: Four scrub points (message, exception values, breadcrumb messages, breadcrumb data) plus a debug-build DSN kill. tracing::error! auto-becomes a Sentry issue and warn! a breadcrumb, so ANY new error log is an egress path — nothing tests that pii::scrub covers a newly logged field.

situations.name: Execution trace instrumentation
situations.definition: A developer adds a phase of work that should be attributable in the execution inspector with timing and cost.
situations.note: Closed SpanType enum + MAX_SPANS eviction; a new phase means editing the enum, which forces the ts-rs binding regen. Startup timing is a separate parallel mechanism with its own OnceLock report.

situations.name: Engine ceilings and caps
situations.definition: A developer bounds a runaway loop, fan-out, batch, or spend and needs the constant plus the clamping helper in the right layer.
situations.note: limits.rs is the canonical home with cap_with_log for observability, but MAX_SPANS, RETENTION, and per-subsystem budget defaults live in their own modules. run_budget is warn-only today — the ceiling is documented as enforcement but does not abort.

situations.name: Documentation sync enforcement
situations.definition: A developer changes user-visible behavior and must update the feature doc, the onboarding tour, and the cross-repo marketing guide in the same session.
situations.note: An agent-facing Stop hook, not a CI gate — it reads the turn transcript and exits 2 with a nag, and a one-sentence dismissal satisfies it. Enforcement therefore depends on the agent choosing not to dismiss; it has its own unit tests, which most gates here do not.

situations.name: i18n key and value gates
situations.definition: A developer adds a user-facing string and needs every locale to have the key AND a genuinely translated value before it ships.
situations.note: Three layers with three different enforcement levels. Key parity: pre-commit strict + CI. Value translation: pre-commit only, NOT in CI, and glob-scoped so it never fires on a JSX-only commit. Route-section coverage — the check that caught 13 fully-translated sections rendering 100% English forever — is wired to NOTHING: no npm script, no hook, no workflow.

situations.name: Bulk translation pipeline
situations.definition: A developer has a translation gap across 13 locales and needs it closed without hand-editing 13 JSON files.
situations.note: Three-step extract → per-locale subagent → merge, where merge refuses any locale that dropped keys or broke a {placeholder} and asserts strict coverage before finishing. One of the few workflows in the repo whose verify step is part of the tool rather than a separate gate.

situations.name: Locale bundle splitting
situations.definition: A developer needs translated strings to load as per-route lazy chunks instead of one 500KB bundle, without an English-first-paint flash.
situations.note: The generated-artifact half is solid; the declaration half (routeSections.ts, which decides whether a section is ever fetched) has no gate, and its failure mode is silent and total — English everywhere for that feature, in every locale, with all other i18n checks green.

situations.name: Bundle and binary size budget
situations.definition: A developer adds a dependency or asset and needs the shipped artifact to stay under a declared size ceiling.
situations.note: Budget is a single shared module consumed by both the gate and the PR-comment reporter, so the two can't disagree. Binary-size budget is separate and only runs during release.

situations.name: Build cache hygiene
situations.definition: A developer's local build gets slow, huge, or mysteriously broken, and needs the right surgical clean rather than a nuclear cargo clean.
situations.note: Deliberately advisory — cache-budget exits 0 unconditionally and refreshes in a detached process so it can never block a build. Recovery is a documented ladder (clean:ort → clean:cache → clean:rust) rather than one command.

situations.name: Parallel session coordination
situations.definition: Multiple CLI agents share one checkout on one branch and need to not clobber each other's uncommitted work.
situations.note: Entirely prose-enforced apart from one real constraint (hooks never mutate the tree). Two documented data-loss incidents — a git stash that swept another session's five files, and a commit that swept 18 pre-staged files under a misleading message — and neither the ledger registration nor the `git diff --cached --stat` verification has any machine check.

situations.name: Agent-facing repo contract
situations.definition: A developer or agent needs to know this repo's canonical build/test/lint/scan commands and hard boundaries without reading prose.
situations.note: Same command on pre-push (primary) and PR CI (backstop) — the cleanest shift-left split in the repo. But every capability is `verified: false`, and ai-conformance triggers on pull_request only while development lands directly on master, so the backstop rarely fires.

situations.name: Duplicated CI systems
situations.definition: A developer adds or changes a gate and must decide whether the second, parallel CI definition also needs it.
situations.note: A full parallel GitLab pipeline (lint/test/security/build-check/binding-drift) duplicates the GitHub gates with materially different content — e.g. it runs `cargo clippy` without the `--features desktop` that GitHub's file documents as mandatory. Nothing keeps the two in sync and no one is told which is authoritative.

situations.name: Theme contrast enforcement
situations.definition: A developer adds or edits a color token and needs every theme's text pairings to still clear WCAG AA.
situations.note: Hard-fails CI on four text-token pairings per theme and only warns on accent/status pairs — an unusually well-calibrated split between must-hold and advisory. Paired with a warn-level lint rule for the per-component half.

situations.name: Shared component boundary
situations.definition: A developer builds a reusable UI primitive and must decide whether it belongs in the catalog and keep it free of app state.
situations.note: Explicitly de-gated by decision: the boundary lint is warn-only, catalog staleness no longer fails `npm run check`, and check:catalog / check:catalog-boundary exist as manual audits only. A rare case where 'no gate' is the intended posture.

situations.name: Conventional commit format
situations.definition: A developer writes a commit message that the changelog generator and release tooling can parse.
situations.note: The canonical example of a gate that ran green while checking nothing: `origin/${base_ref}..HEAD` expands to an invalid revision on push events, so the job exited 128 on every push (the primary trigger) rather than reporting a verdict.
